summary: This Wikipedia-style article introduces Iran as a sovereign state in Western Asia and traces its history from early civilizations such as Elam through the Median, Achaemenid, Parthian, and Sassanid empires, the Arab conquest and Islamization, the Qajar dynasty, and the 1979 hostage crisis. It also covers the country's geography, population and ethnic makeup, religions, and cultural and energy significance. The note emphasizes the Achaemenid Empire's size and administration and Iran's role in the Islamic Golden Age.
one_line: Overview of Iran's geography, population, religions, and history from ancient Elamite and Achaemenid times through the Islamic era to the modern Islamic Republic.
key_facts: The Islamic Golden Age reached its peak by the 10th and 11th centuries, during which Iran was the main theater of the scientific activities.
After the 10th century, Persian language, alongside Arabic, was used for the scientific, philosophical, historical, musical, and medical works.
Iran has a land area of 1,648,195 km2 (636,372 sq mi), making it the second-largest country in the Middle East and the 18th-largest in the world.
With 78.4 million inhabitants, Iran is the world's 17th-most-populous country.
Iran is the only country that has both a Caspian Sea and an Indian Ocean coastline.
Cyrus the Great took over the Median Empire in 550 BC and founded the Achaemenid Empire by unifying other city states.
Alexander the Great defeated the last Achaemenid emperor, Darius III, at the Battle of Issus in 334 BC.
The Achaemenid Empire collapsed in 330 BC following the conquests of Alexander the Great.
The Sassanid Dynasty succeeded the Parthian Empire in 224 AD, and Iran again became one of the leading powers in the world for more than four centuries.
Aqa Mohammad Khan founded the Qajar Dynasty in 1794 after a civil war that followed the death of Karim Khan in 1779.
On November 4, 1979, a group of students seized the United States Embassy and took 52 personnel and citizens hostage.
The Algiers Accords led to the release of the last hostages on Jimmy Carter's final day in office.
Tehran is the country's capital and largest city, as well as its leading cultural and economic center.
Iran has 19 UNESCO World Heritage Sites, the fourth-largest number in Asia and 12th-largest in the world.
Christianity, Judaism, Zoroastrianism, and the Sunni branch of Islam are officially recognized by the government, while the Baha'i Faith is not officially recognized.
